catalog_citation: SIL-PNG, Organised Phonology Data: Siane (Komogu) Language [SNP], data checked by Dorothy James (2002); corroborated by James, Dorothy J. 1994. 'Word tone in a Papuan language: an autosegmental solution.' Language and Linguistics in Melanesia 25:125-148.
catalog_locator: OPD p.3, section 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)'; James 1994 p.126 section 2 'Tones, Vowel Sequences, and Timing'
catalog_quote: Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length) Normally the first syllable of each word is stressed, with alternate following syllables receiving secondary stress. In addition, the final high tone of a series of highs preceding a low tone receives primary stress, a syllable carrying a tone glide receives primary stress, and the verb negative suffix -am is stressed with high tone. There is no contrastive lengthening of either vowels or consonants in any dialect of Siane. There are five main contrastive word tone patterns: high /H/, low /L/, high-low /HL/, low-high /LH/ and high-low-high /HLH/. For a full description of the Siane Komogu suprasegmental system, including syllable structure and timing features, with many examples, see James, 1994. ... [James 1994:126, scanned] Siane makes significant use of tone to distinguish between lexical items.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Siane has an empty rule and there are no existing statements, so nothing is contradicted; this source supplies the rule: a tone language (H/L) with a default initial primary stress, alternating secondary stress, and tone-conditioned stress shifts. Describes the Komogu dialect (fn. 2, p. 12).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Siane has two tone phonemes, high (acute) and low (unmarked), contrasting on every syllable (sec. 1.3, pp. 13-14). Stress is a separate, non-contrastive layer: by default the first syllable of the word carries primary stress, with secondary stresses on every other following syllable (alternating from the initial). Tone overrides this default: the last high of a run of highs in a word or pause group takes primary stress (and is raised in pitch), a syllable with a contour (diverse tone sequence on a geminate vowel cluster) takes primary stress, and the negative verb suffix -ám is stressed with high tone; these can shift the primary stress or add one or two further primaries. Sec. 2.2 adds that non-contrastive half-length often falls on the vowel of a stressed syllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Stated explicitly: 'secondary stress occurring on alternate following syllables' after the initial primary (p. 15, sec. 2.4), i.e. a left-to-right binary alternation.
new_statements.exceptions: (a) the final high tone of a series of highs within a word or pause group receives primary stress (sec. 2.3); (b) the verb negative suffix -ám is stressed with high tone; (c) a syllable carrying diverse (contour) tones receives primary stress; these cause a stress shift or one or two additional primary stresses (sec. 2.4). Fn. 7 (p. 15): 'It is expected that additional conditioning factors of stress patterning will be found on further study of higher level phonology.' Fn. 10 (p. 16): in some reduplicated words with an apparent syllable division inside a diverse vowel cluster, 'the normal stress pattern of the word seems to fall on the second of the two vowels rather than on the next following syllable'.
new_statements.identity_note: James & Lucht 1962 state (fn. 2, p. 12) that the analysis is based on the Komogu dialect of Siane, with data gathered over fourteen months in a village near the Watabung patrol post, Eastern Highlands; they name five major dialects (Komogu, Labau, Ono, Kolepa, Yafiyufa) and note that Wurm separates Yafiyufa from the rest of Siane. Fn. 4 notes the Kolepa dialect uses the glottal stop more extensively than Komogu.

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: Both deciding quotations are present verbatim in copies we hold at the stated locators (OPD p.3 Suprasegmentals; James 1994 p.126 sec. 2). The classification 'tonal' with non-contrastive, partly tone-conditioned default-initial stress rests on the principal fieldworker's own tonal phonology article (1994, 24 pp., 33 years of fieldwork) and her 2002 OPD summary; Glottolog lists no reference grammar and no later phonology, and the SIL [snp] resource list (2015 snapshot) shows nothing newer on phonology than the OPD. Cahill 2011 (downloaded now, open) independently summarises Siane as classical word tone from James 1994, confirming the classification and silent on stress. Remaining unheld items are short 1960s-70s pieces by the same SIL team, superseded by James 1994; none is likely to change the classification.

sources.quote: 'Siane (Trans-New Guinea) has H, L, HL, and LH patterns on mono-, di-, and trisyllabic words, and HLH on all but monosyllabic ones ... (James 1994). Diphthongs are short and act as single TBUs. Most suffixes are toneless and receive their tone by spreading from the last tone of the root. Siane exhibits classical autosegmental behavior in that when a vowel is elided, its tone persists.' No statement about stress.
